chunks: In a non-inverting amplifier the signal goes straight into the op-amp's plus input, which has an enormous impedance, megaohms or more, so it doesn't load the source.
In an inverting amplifier the input impedance is just the input resistor, because the minus node is a virtual ground.

If my source is a sensor with ten kilohms of output resistance and my input resistor is also ten kilohms, I've lost half my signal in a divider, and that source resistance also becomes part of the gain equation.
With a non-inverting stage, the source resistance doesn't matter to the gain.
Other advantages: the output isn't inverted, so there's no phase flip to worry about, and I can set the gain to exactly one with a buffer, which is how I isolate a high-impedance node from a load.
For the same noise gain the bandwidth is also a little better: a non-inverting gain of 10 has a noise gain of 10, whereas an inverting gain of minus 10 has a noise gain of 11.
But it's not always better. The non-inverting circuit can't have a gain below one.
And both inputs swing with the signal, so I need to stay inside the common-mode range and the CMRR error adds to the signal.
The inverting configuration keeps both inputs at a fixed voltage, which is why it's the choice for summing amplifiers, precision DC work and current-to-voltage conversion.
So it's input impedance and source type that decide."
